1212.title: What they share
1212.hook: Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story
1212.howItsDone: Jews from different movements read the same Torah, keep the same weekly Shabbat and yearly festivals, and often speak of klal Yisrael, the whole community of Israel, across their differences.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: many streams. Modern Jews organize themselves in movements, and no single one speaks for all. Before walking through them one by one, a step back.

A long table on a spring night. One cousin wears a black hat. Another drove in from a congregation with a different prayer book. A third hasn't been inside a synagogue in years. Someone at the far end has a kippah that keeps sliding off. Then the youngest child stands and asks the question the seder sets for the youngest: why is this night different from all other nights? And every head turns toward the same answer, the same story of slaves who walked out of Egypt. The streams run in different channels. Today is about the water they carry together.
screen: `ONE TABLE, MANY COUSINS.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `THE SAME STORY.`

segments.voice: What they share. Five things, one for each finger. First, Torah. The streams read the same five books, and hear the same line at their heart: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD." They argue about how the Torah came to be and how to live it; that's tomorrow. But the scroll in the ark is the same scroll. Second, Shabbat. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." One family keeps every detail of the law. Another lights candles and turns off the phones for dinner. It's still the seventh day, and it still begins at sundown on Friday. Third, the festivals. "These are the feasts of the LORD," Leviticus says, and it lists them: Passover, the counting to Shavuot, the new year, the Day of Atonement, Sukkot. Different prayer books, same calendar. Fourth, the people. When Ruth joins her mother-in-law, she doesn't only say your God. She says "thy people shall be my people" first. In her line, belonging to a family comes before the creed. Fifth, the story: Abraham and Sarah, the slavery, the sea, Sinai, the land, the exile, the long road home. The streams tell it in different keys, and each tells it as its own. A Hebrew phrase holds all of this: klal Yisrael, the whole community of Israel. Not one movement; all of them. Psalm 133 says: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Unity, there, doesn't mean sameness. It means sitting at one table.
screen: `TORAH: THE SAME SCROLL.` · `SHABBAT: THE SAME SEVENTH DAY.` · `THE FESTIVALS: ONE CALENDAR.` · `THE PEOPLE AND ITS STORY.` · then, large: `KLAL YISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Hold up one hand, fingers open, and fold one finger on each breath: Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people, the story. Then open your hand and go around once more, slower, picturing for each finger one face you know, Jewish or not, who has something to do with it: a neighbor's candles, a friend's seder.
What they share. Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story: five things the streams of Judaism hold, even when they hold them differently. Today's word.
Your line: more in common. Different prayer books, and still one long table. See you tomorrow.

1213.title: What they debate
1213.hook: how revelation works, how binding halakha is, and how change happens
1213.howItsDone: The movements of modern Judaism differ mainly over how revelation works, how binding halakha is, and who may change practice and how; each answers these questions in its own literature and its own rabbinical bodies.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: more in common. Torah, Shabbat, the festivals, the people and its story, on five fingers. Now the other hand.

An argument about an oven, in the Talmud. Rabbi Eliezer stands alone against the other sages. If I am right, he says, let this carob tree prove it, and the tree tears itself up and moves. A tree proves nothing, they answer. Let the stream prove it, and the water flows backward. Let the walls of the study hall prove it, and the walls start to lean. At last a voice from heaven: the law follows Eliezer. And Rabbi Joshua stands up and quotes Deuteronomy: it is not in heaven. The Talmud adds that God laughed and said, my children have defeated me. Today: the questions under that story.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT AN OVEN.` → `A TREE, A STREAM, THE WALLS.` → `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: What they debate. Three questions, and one under all three. First: how does revelation work? The Mishnah draws a hard line here: among those it says lose their share in the world to come is the one who denies that the Torah is from heaven, in Hebrew Torah min ha-shamayim. Some Jews hold that God gave the Torah, word for word, to Moses at Sinai. Some hold that God's revelation came through human beings, over time, with human hands and voices in it. Some hold views in between. And they still read from the same kind of scroll on Shabbat morning. Second: how binding is halakha, Jewish law? For some, the law is a command, as binding today as when it was given. For others, it's a precious inheritance that guides but doesn't finally decide; a person weighs it with conscience and community. Third: how does change happen? When the world changes, electricity, new medicine, new roles for women, who may adjust the practice, and how? A recognized scholar, ruling from earlier rulings? A committee? Each community? Each person? Now the question under all three: who gets to say? The commandment, Deuteronomy says, "is not in heaven." It is near, in your mouth and in your heart. Some read it the way Rabbi Joshua did: the law now lives with its human interpreters. Others read it as: it was given clearly, so it can be kept. The same verse holds both. Soon each movement gets its own day, in its own words.
screen: `HOW DOES REVELATION WORK?` · `HOW BINDING IS HALAKHA?` · `HOW DOES CHANGE HAPPEN?` · `WHO GETS TO SAY?` · then, large: `IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one rule you live by, from a tradition, a parent, a teacher or your own conscience. Ask it the three questions gently: where did it come from, how binding is it for you, and who would get to change it? Notice which one felt hardest, then let it go.
What they debate. How revelation works, how binding halakha is, and how change happens: three questions, and under them, who gets to say. Today's word.
Your line: the questions. Under most arguments sits a question worth naming. That's today, done.

1214.title: Orthodox Judaism
1214.hook: holds the Torah as divinely given and halakha as binding
1214.howItsDone: Orthodox Jews keep halakha as binding, including Shabbat, kashrut, daily prayer and blessings before and after eating, and bring new questions to rabbis who answer from the Talmud, the codes and earlier rulings.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the questions. How revelation works, how binding halakha is, how change happens, and under them, who gets to say. Today, the first answer.

An apple on a kitchen counter. A teenager grabs it on the way out the door, already late, phone in the other hand. Before the first bite, she stops. A few Hebrew words under her breath, a blessing for the fruit of the tree, and then the crunch. It takes about as long as a red light. Nobody is watching. She says it anyway, because in her home that pause is not a nice idea. It is the law, and the law is binding, the same as on any other morning.
screen: `AN APPLE, A LATE TEENAGER.` → `A BLESSING BEFORE THE BITE.` → `NOT A NICE IDEA. THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Orthodox Judaism. Take yesterday's three questions and hear its answers. First, revelation. Orthodox Jews hold that the Torah is from heaven: given by God to Moses. And not only the written scroll. An oral teaching came with it, explaining how to live the written words, and it was handed down. The Mishnah's tractate of the Fathers opens with that chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. Second, halakha. Because the source is divine, the law is binding. Shabbat, the dietary laws, prayer, blessings like the teenager's: these are commandments, kept today as they were kept before. Deuteronomy says: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it." Third, change. Orthodoxy doesn't say nothing ever changes. New questions arrive constantly: an elevator on Shabbat, a new medicine, a new food additive. A trained rabbi answers them from inside the law, reasoning from the Talmud, the codes like the Shulchan Aruch, and the rulings of earlier scholars. The answer can be new. The method and the authority stay within the tradition. Fourth, Orthodoxy is not one community. Soon you'll meet several streams inside it, each with its own style. What holds them together is today's line. For Orthodox Jews, the tradition isn't something they own. It binds them, and they are bound to it.
screen: `TORAH FROM HEAVEN, WRITTEN AND ORAL.` · `THE LAW IS BINDING.` · `NEW QUESTIONS, OLD METHOD.` · `MANY STREAMS INSIDE ORTHODOXY.` · then, large: `YE SHALL NOT ADD, NEITHER DIMINISH.`

segments.voice: If there's a cup of water or something to eat nearby, set it in front of you, or picture it, and before you take it, stop and notice the urge to reach. Notice where it came from, the hands and the rain behind it. If you pray, say a blessing you already know; if not, let the pause stand for a few breaths, then drink or eat slowly.
Orthodox Judaism. The movement that holds the Torah, written and oral, as given by God, and halakha as binding, with new questions answered from inside the law. Today's word.

1215.title: Haredi Judaism
1215.hook: "those who tremble": close-knit communities devoted to Torah study
1215.howItsDone: Haredi Jews keep halakha in full and build close-knit communities around Torah study, with yeshivas for young men, kollels for married men, schools for girls and women, and strong networks of mutual help.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: binding tradition. Orthodox Judaism holds the Torah as given by God and halakha as binding, with several streams inside it. Today, the first stream.

Close to midnight, and the room is still full: tables, open books, and noise. Two people lean over one page of Talmud, and one is jabbing the margin with a finger. Across the table, another pair argues the same line from the other side. Nobody shushes anybody. This is a study hall, a beit midrash, and in today's communities, a room like this sits near the center of life. From outside, people tend to notice the dark coats and hats. From inside, people tend to talk about the page.
screen: `A LOUD ROOM OF BOOKS.` → `TWO PEOPLE, ONE PAGE.` → `THE PAGE AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Haredi. First, the name comes from a verse. Isaiah says: "Hear the word of the LORD, ye that tremble at his word." In Hebrew, those who tremble is haredim. So the name isn't about fear of people. It describes awe before the word of God, a seriousness that shapes a whole life. Second, study. God tells Joshua the book of the law should not leave his mouth: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." Haredi communities take that line close to literally. Boys and young men may spend long years in a yeshiva, and some married men keep learning in a kollel, a study hall for adults, while the family's life is arranged to support it. Women learn too, in their own schools, and in some families carry much of the work outside the home. Third, community. Haredi life is close-knit on purpose: its own schools, its own neighborhoods, a careful distance from much of the wider culture's media. Inside, there are free-loan funds, meals brought to new mothers, and help for anyone in trouble. And it isn't one thing. Some communities are Hasidic, gathered around a rebbe. Others center on the yeshivas and their heads. There are Sephardi Haredi communities too. Fourth, why study holds that place. The Mishnah lists good deeds whose fruit a person enjoys in this world, honoring parents, acts of kindness, making peace between people, and ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all. Elsewhere the sages ask which is greater, study or doing, and answer: study, because study leads to doing. In this view, the open book is where every other good thing begins.
screen: `YE THAT TREMBLE AT HIS WORD.` · `DAY AND NIGHT: A LIFE OF STUDY.` · `CLOSE-KNIT ON PURPOSE.` · `STUDY LEADS TO DOING.` · then, large: `DEVOTED STUDY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose life is shaped by a devotion you don't share: a religious neighbor, an athlete in training, a grandparent who never missed a morning prayer. Leave aside whether you'd live that way, and look at what it costs them, and what it gives them. If you pray, you can hold them in that prayer.
Haredi. Those who tremble at God's word, from Isaiah: close-knit communities, Hasidic and others, that put the study of Torah at the center of life. Today's word.
Your line: devoted study. Awe before the word can shape a whole life. See you tomorrow.

1216.title: Modern Orthodoxy
1216.hook: full halakha joined with engagement in the wider world
1216.howItsDone: Modern Orthodox Jews keep halakha in full while studying and working in the wider world, often in schools that teach Jewish texts alongside secular subjects.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Haredi: those who tremble at God's word, and your line, devoted study. Today, another Orthodox stream, keeping the same law with a different door open.

Six in the morning, a hospital stairwell. A resident in green scrubs, at the end of a long night shift, has a small prayer book open against the railing. She's saying the morning prayers before rounds, between the vending machine and the fire door. In an hour she'll present cases to her attending. Tonight she'll light Shabbat candles. Nothing in her day is split into a religious half and a worldly half. She'd say it's one life. Today, the stream that tries to live that way.
screen: `A STAIRWELL AT SIX A.M.` → `SCRUBS AND A PRAYER BOOK.` → `ONE LIFE, NOT TWO HALVES.`

segments.voice: Modern Orthodoxy. Full halakha, and the whole world too. First, the law is not lighter. Modern Orthodox Jews keep Shabbat, keep kosher, pray, and hold the Torah as given by God, just as yesterday's communities do. The difference isn't how much of the law, but how open the door to the wider world is. Second, an old line. In the tractate of the Fathers, Rabban Gamliel teaches that Torah study is excellent when joined with derekh eretz, a worldly occupation, the way of the land. Torah without work, he says, ends up empty. Third, a modern teacher. Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik, a Modern Orthodox thinker, read the first chapters of Genesis as two portraits of one person. The first Adam is told to "replenish the earth, and subdue it": build, discover, master the world. The second Adam is placed in the garden "to dress it and to keep it": to serve, to belong, to stand before God. A person of faith, he taught, is called to be both, and the two never fully settle. Fourth, what that looks like. Secular university next to the study hall. Science next to Talmud. A career, a vote, a seat at the table of public life, and a full Shabbat. Some call it Torah and worldly knowledge; some, Torah with the way of the land. And it carries real tensions, which its own thinkers argue about openly: how far to engage, and where to hold the line. The resident in the stairwell holds both books. Modern Orthodoxy says that's the point.
screen: `THE LAW IS NOT LIGHTER.` · `TORAH WITH THE WAY OF THE LAND.` · `TWO ADAMS, ONE PERSON.` · `ONE LIFE, AND ITS TENSIONS.` · then, large: `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next real task waiting for you, an email, a shift, a class, the dishes, and take one of today's lines into it: to dress it and to keep it, to serve the thing in front of you, not only to master it. Picture yourself doing it that way, with care, start to finish. If you pray, you can hold the task up in that prayer.
Modern Orthodoxy. Full halakha joined with engagement in the wider world: Torah with the way of the land, two Adams in one person. Today's word.

1217.title: Religious Zionism
1217.hook: an Orthodox stream that sees the State of Israel as religiously significant
1217.howItsDone: Religious Zionists keep halakha in full and recite a prayer for the State of Israel in synagogue, and some combine Torah study with national service and mark Israel's Independence Day with psalms of praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Modern Orthodoxy, and your line: torah and the world, full halakha with the door open. Today, a stream that looks at one place in that world in a particular way.

"When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream." Psalm 126. Tradition sets it at the table, sung before grace on Shabbat and festivals, a song about a homecoming so sudden it felt unreal. Now take that psalm into a synagogue where, after the Torah reading, the congregation stands for a prayer for the State of Israel. For the people in that room, the psalm's dream isn't only a memory or a hope. They read it as something beginning to happen in their own time.
screen: `WE WERE LIKE THEM THAT DREAM.` → `A PRAYER FOR THE STATE.` → `A DREAM BEGINNING NOW.`

segments.voice: Religious Zionism. First, it's Orthodox. Religious Zionists keep halakha in full and hold the Torah as given by God. What marks them out is how they understand the State of Israel. Second, the reading. The prophets promise a return. Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the psalms: the exiles gathered, the land rebuilt. Religious Zionists see the return of Jews to the land, and the state that grew from it, as part of that promise unfolding, a religious event and not only a political one. Third, a teacher. Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, a teacher this stream looks to, taught something that surprised some: that even pioneers who had left religious practice behind, draining swamps and planting fields, were taking part in a holy process without knowing it. The prayer said for the state in these synagogues calls it reshit tzmichat geulatenu: the first flowering of our redemption. Not the redemption complete, but its beginning. Fourth, what it looks like. Study halls where young people combine Torah learning with national service. Holidays marked with the psalms of praise. A love of the land itself, its hills and its harvests, as a commandment. And not every Jew shares this view. Some Haredi communities hold that redemption must wait for the Messiah, and see the state differently. Other Jews value Israel for reasons that aren't religious at all. This lesson is one stream's view, in its own words, not politics, and it ranks no one.
screen: `FULLY ORTHODOX.` · `THE PROPHETS' RETURN, UNFOLDING.` · `HOLINESS IN THE PLOWING.` · `NOT EVERY JEW READS IT THIS WAY.` · then, large: `THE FIRST FLOWERING OF OUR REDEMPTION.`

segments.voice: Take one phrase, the first flowering, and say it to yourself slowly, then the psalm's line: we were like them that dream. Whatever you think about the politics of the place, try for these minutes to hear how the words sound to someone who prays them: a hope very old, and something beginning. Hold the two phrases side by side, without arguing with them.

1218.title: Sephardi and Mizrahi practice
1218.hook: often less divided into movements, with traditional practice across a wide range
1218.howItsDone: Sephardi and Mizrahi communities keep their own melodies, prayer order and customs, often following the rulings of the Shulchan Aruch, and their synagogues are frequently traditional while welcoming people of varied observance.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: religious zionism, an Orthodox stream that reads the State of Israel as the first flowering of redemption. Today closes the week with a different kind of map.

A tall case of carved silver stands on the reader's table. Someone unlatches it and swings it open like a cabinet, and there is the Torah scroll, upright, facing the room. The case is called a tik. In the rows facing it sits a man who keeps every detail of Shabbat and walked here, and next to him his nephew, who drove, parked around the corner, and is singing louder than anyone. They pray from the same book, to the tunes their families brought from far away. Nobody checks a label at the door.
screen: `A SCROLL STANDING IN ITS CASE.` → `ONE WALKED, ONE DROVE.` → `NO LABEL AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Sephardi and Mizrahi practice. You met the Sephardim on day nine hundred forty-six, and Mizrahi Jews on day nine hundred eighty-seven. Today, how they practice. First, the names. Obadiah speaks of "the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad." Tradition came to read Sepharad as Spain, and Sephardi Jews trace their families to Spain and Portugal, and from there to North Africa, the Ottoman lands and beyond. Mizrahi comes from mizrach, east, the word in the psalm's "as far as the east is from the west." Mizrahi Jews come from lands like Iraq, Iran, Yemen and Syria. The two words overlap, and families use them differently. Second, the law. Rabbi Joseph Karo wrote the Shulchan Aruch largely following Sephardi practice. Rabbi Moses Isserles added notes for Ashkenazi Jews, printed on the same page. One code, two customs, side by side. Third, the movements. The split into Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others grew up among Ashkenazi Jews in Europe and America. Often, in Sephardi and Mizrahi communities, the synagogue stayed traditional, and people across a wide range of personal observance kept coming, without anyone needing a new label. Fourth, the custom. The tik is one: carved wood in some synagogues, silver in others, the scroll inside read standing, like a book set on its spine. Small things like that, melodies, foods, the order of prayers, carry a home across centuries and borders. The week ends here, where tradition is less a position than a house.
screen: `SEPHARAD AND THE EAST.` · `ONE CODE, TWO CUSTOMS.` · `LESS DIVIDED INTO MOVEMENTS.` · `THE TORAH STANDING IN ITS CASE.` · then, large: `TRADITION AS HOME.`

segments.voice: Picture the scroll standing upright in its case, the doors opening like a cabinet. Then bring to mind one custom from your own family, a dish, a song, a way of setting the table, that came from somewhere far away. Hold the two side by side, and notice how a small thing carries a whole place.

Sephardi and Mizrahi practice. Jewish life from Spain, North Africa and the lands to the east: often less divided into movements, with traditional synagogues that welcome a wide range of observance. Today's word.
Your line: tradition as home. Some doors never needed a label. Rest well.
